Selection rule: the current conversation — session memory; durable facts about you — long-term; huge documents — external.
Remember: each type solves its own job. Trying to stuff everything into one is the path to overpaying and clutter.
s3.validate: You can name the three memory types and give an example for each of when it fits.
s3.tip: If you ask yourself "should AI remember this always or only in this chat?" — you're already choosing between long-term and session memory.

s4.title: How Claude remembers context
s4.why: Theory becomes useful when you see it in a concrete tool. Claude has built-in ways to give AI long-term and project memory.
instructions: Memory: Claude can save durable facts about you and your work and pull them into new conversations — that's long-term memory. More — [[node:cap-memory|Memory]].
Projects: inside a project Claude keeps shared context and files available across all chats of that project. So conversations stop starting from scratch.
The difference matters: session memory lives in one chat; Memory and projects carry knowledge between chats.
What goes where: personal preferences and stable facts — into Memory; documents and materials of specific work — into project files.
Remember: you decide what Claude should remember long-term. It doesn't happen magically — you set it up.
s4.validate: You can explain the difference between what Claude remembers in one chat and what carries over via Memory and projects.
s4.tip: If you catch yourself repeating the same thing to Claude in every chat — that's a signal to move it into Memory or a project.

s5.title: Tricks against "forgetting"
s5.why: Knowing the cause, you can act. A few simple tricks greatly reduce the "AI forgot everything" effect in real work.
instructions: Summary: when a conversation is long, ask AI to briefly summarize the agreements. A short summary takes little space and keeps the essence.
/compact: in a long session this command compresses the past conversation, freeing space in the window without losing the main points.
External documents: keep important materials in project files or a knowledge base rather than pasting them as a wall into every chat.
Explicit context up front: if a task needs facts, give them at the start of the request — don't rely on AI "remembering" from last time.
Remember the combo: short summary + external documents + Memory cover most "forgetting" problems.
s5.validate: You can name at least three tricks and say which problem each solves.
s5.tip: Before closing an important session, ask for a short summary of decisions — that's your "episodic memory" for next time.

s6.title: Limits and verification
s6.why: To avoid disappointment, it's important to understand the honest limits of AI memory and to be able to check that it really "remembers".
instructions: Remember the limit: even a large context window is finite, and long-term memory holds only what you saved — not everything.
Don't rely on "AI surely remembers". If a fact is critical — give it explicitly or check that it's in Memory or the project.
Verification: ask AI what it remembers about the task. If the answer is inaccurate — the needed context isn't on the "desk" and must be added.
Stale-data danger: long-term memory can hold old facts. Periodically check that AI relies on what's current.

Put it together: the cause of "forgetting" is the context window; the solution is the right memory type (session, long-term via [[node:cap-memory|Memory]], external via [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]) plus tricks.
s6.validate: You can check what exactly AI remembers about a task and understand where the boundary of its memory lies.
s6.tip: A simple test: ask "what do you remember about my project?". The answer shows what's really in memory versus what you only thought you saved.

af-multimodal.title: Multimodal AI — a model that sees and hears
af-multimodal.subtitle: How AI works not only with text but with images too, and where its limits are
af-multimodal.whatItIs: Ordinary AI used to work only with text. Multimodal AI understands several data types at once in a single request: text together with images (as well as audio and video). You can show the model a screenshot, a photo, a diagram — and it describes what it sees and answers your question.
af-multimodal.approach: We move from concept to practice: first what "multimodality" even means, then how the model "sees" an image in plain terms. Next, what it does well versus poorly, and how to use it in Claude via [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] and [[node:cap-input-modalities|input modalities]]. Finally, the limits and how to verify the result. Conceptual, no code.
outcomes: You understand what "multimodality" means: text and images in one request
You can explain in plain terms how the model "sees" an image
You know which visual tasks AI handles well and which it handles poorly
You can apply it in Claude: show a screenshot, photo, or diagram and ask a question
You see the limits of the technology and verify the answer instead of trusting blindly

applyIn.title: Parsing screenshots and errors
applyIn.description: Show a screenshot of an error or interface and ask "what's wrong here?" instead of retyping the text by hand.

applyIn.title: Reading documents and receipts
applyIn.description: A photo of an invoice, receipt, or table — AI recognizes amounts and dates and transfers the data, saving manual work.

applyIn.title: Understanding diagrams and mockups
applyIn.description: Show a chart from a report or a design mockup — AI describes the trend or helps build a page from the picture.

pitfalls: Thinking "AI sees everything like a human" — in reality there are weak spots
Asking it to read tiny or handwritten text — specialized OCR does this better
Expecting pixel precision: counting objects in a photo exactly is something the model does worse
Loading a busy diagram with a dozen lines and trusting the answer without checking
Using multimodality where the task is purely textual — that's needless overhead

exercises.question: How does multimodal AI differ from ordinary text AI — in one sentence?
exercises.hint: It's about data types: text vs. "text + images and other types in one request".

exercises.question: Name two tasks where the model "sees" well, and two where it does poorly.
exercises.hint: Well: objects in photos, printed text. Poorly: handwriting, exact counting, an overloaded chart.

exercises.question: Someone sent you an error screenshot. How does multimodality save time versus the "old way"?
exercises.hint: No need to retype the error text by hand — you drop in the image and ask right away.

s1.title: What "multimodality" means
s1.why: Without this concept it's easy to confuse multimodal AI with ordinary AI or expect too much. A modality is a data type: text, image, audio, video.
instructions: Remember the simple definition: a "modality" = a data type. Text is one modality, an image is another.
Multimodal AI takes several types at once: for example, the text of your question together with an attached image.
Compare: with ordinary AI you write "translate this article". With multimodal AI you attach a screenshot and write "what's wrong here?".
Recall the related concept in Atlas — [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI fundamentals]] — to see where this topic fits.
s1.validate: You can say in your own words that multimodality is working with text and images (and other types) in a single request.
s1.tip: The word "modality" sounds complex, but it just means a "channel of perception": like a human has sight and hearing.

s2.title: How the model "sees" an image
s2.why: Understanding the mechanics in plain terms removes the magic and helps you predict where the model will fail.
instructions: Imagine the model doesn't "look with eyes" but turns the picture into a set of numbers — features of shape, color, and text in it.
From these features it looks for patterns it was trained on: "this looks like a button", "this is a line of code", "this is a chart".
Text and image land in one shared "understanding" — that's why you can ask about the image in words.
Remember the key point: this is pattern recognition, not exact "reading of pixels".
s2.validate: You can explain that the model converts the picture into features and matches them against what it learned, rather than "seeing" like a human.
s2.tip: Analogy: the model "recognizes" the familiar in a picture rather than measuring it with a ruler.

s3.title: What it does well
s3.why: Knowing the strengths lets you apply AI right where it genuinely saves time.
instructions: Describing an image: "what's in this picture?" — the model confidently lists objects and the scene.
Parsing a screenshot: an interface, an error message, a long stack trace — it finds where the problem is.
Diagrams and charts of medium complexity: it describes the trend and explains what an axis shows.
Printed text in a photo: it recognizes amounts on a receipt, headings, captions.
Try it yourself: show AI a screenshot of any screen and ask it to describe what's visible.
s3.validate: You can name at least three tasks where the model "sees" reliably: description, parsing a screenshot, reading printed text.
s3.tip: The clearer and larger the image, the more accurate the answer — send a good-quality screenshot.

s4.title: What it does poorly
s4.why: Weak spots are a source of silent errors. If you don't know them, it's easy to trust a wrong answer.
instructions: Tiny text: the model may "guess" blurry characters instead of reading them exactly.
Handwritten text: specialized OCR tools handle it better.
Exact counting: "how many people are in the photo?" is a frequent source of errors.
Overloaded diagrams with a dozen lines and labels — high risk of mixing things up.
Pixel precision (coordinates, exact colors) — not a strong point.
s4.validate: You can name at least three cases where the model shouldn't be trusted without checking: tiny/handwritten text, exact counting, complex charts.
s4.tip: If the task falls into a weak zone — don't drop AI entirely, but always double-check the answer.

s5.title: How to use it in Claude
s5.why: Theory without practice is useless. In Claude, multimodality is available right in the chat.
instructions: Attach an image to your message — a screenshot, photo, diagram — and ask your question in words.
In Claude this works through the [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] capability — the model "sees" the attached picture.
The input data types themselves are described as [[node:cap-input-modalities|input modalities]]: exactly what the model can accept as input.
Phrase the question specifically: not "look at the picture" but "find the line with the error" or "extract the amount and date".
Start simple: drop in an error screenshot and ask it to explain what the problem is.
s5.validate: You attached an image in Claude, asked a specific question, and got a meaningful answer about the picture.
s5.tip: One precise question about a picture beats a vague "what do you think?" — the model answers to the request.

s6.title: Limits and verification
s6.why: Mature use = knowing the limit of the technology and building in a check, rather than trusting the answer blindly.
instructions: Remember the main mistake: "multimodal AI sees everything like a human" — that's not true.
Before trusting it, ask yourself: is the task in a strong zone (description, printed text) or a weak one (tiny font, exact counting)?
For important data (amounts, numbers) always check the answer against the original with your own eyes.
Test on your own task types — generic promises that "AI can do everything" don't replace verification.
If the answer is critical — ask the model to show exactly what in the picture it relies on.
s6.validate: You have a habit: before trusting an answer, identify the zone (strong/weak) and re-check important numbers against the original.
s6.tip: The rule is simple: AI speeds you up, but keep the final check of important data for yourself.

af-fine-tuning.title: Fine-tuning vs Prompting — train or explain
af-fine-tuning.subtitle: When to train the model and when a good prompt is enough
af-fine-tuning.whatItIs: A course on two ways to make AI do what you need: **prompting** (explain the task in text) and **fine-tuning** (train the model on your own data). We'll cover the difference, when fine-tuning is truly justified, and why 90% of tasks are solved without it — via [[node:prompting|prompt engineering]] and [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]].
af-fine-tuning.approach: We move from concepts to decision. First a clear line between "train" and "explain", then what fine-tuning is and what it costs, then the ladder for choosing a tool. We finish with common mistakes and a quick "do I even need fine-tuning" check. Conceptual, no code or math.
outcomes: Explain the difference between fine-tuning and prompting in your own words
Understand when fine-tuning is genuinely needed versus wasted spend
Know the choice ladder: prompt → few-shot → RAG → fine-tune
Estimate the real cost and complexity of fine-tuning before you start
Stop confusing "trendy" with "needed" when picking an approach

applyIn.title: Style and tone of replies
applyIn.description: You need AI to answer in your brand voice. Examples in the prompt first; fine-tune only if the style won't transfer via few-shot.

applyIn.title: Narrow domain with data
applyIn.description: Medicine, law, support with thousands of question-answer pairs. Here fine-tuning may pay off — but check RAG first.

applyIn.title: Cutting production cost
applyIn.description: Fine-tune a small model so it replaces a big one on a narrow task and lowers per-request cost.

pitfalls: Fine-tuning "just in case" from day one — like tuning a car you haven't driven yet
Thinking fine-tuning = "AI gets smarter". It's specialization, not an upgrade
Ignoring tech debt: a new model version makes your old fine-tune obsolete
Fine-tuning where a prompt + RAG would do — a wasted quarter and budget
Skipping prompting and few-shot before reaching for fine-tuning

exercises.question: Your task: AI sorts incoming emails into 5 categories. Do you try fine-tuning or prompting first, and why?
exercises.hint: Think about how many examples it takes to explain 5 categories and whether they fit right inside the prompt.

exercises.question: A team spent a quarter fine-tuning, and a month later a better model shipped. What was the planning mistake?
exercises.hint: Recall what happens to a fine-tuned model when a newer base version is released.

exercises.question: Name the three rungs worth climbing before fine-tuning, in the right order.
exercises.hint: The ladder starts with the cheapest, fastest tool and ends with the most expensive one.

s1.title: The difference: train or explain
s1.why: Without a clear line between prompting and fine-tuning, any tool choice is guesswork.
instructions: Picture a new hire: prompting = give instructions each time, fine-tuning = train for months so they just know.
Write in one line what prompting changes (the instruction text) and what fine-tuning changes (the model itself).
Note: prompting is flexible and instant; fine-tuning is slow and locks behavior into the model's weights.
Tie it to basics: review [[node:ai-fundamentals|how AI works]] to see what changes inside.
s1.validate: You can explain the difference in 30 seconds without the word "neural network".
s1.tip: Simple test: if a decision changes by editing text — that's prompting.

s2.title: What fine-tuning is and when it's truly needed
s2.why: Fine-tuning sounds like magic, but it's a narrow tool with three honest scenarios.
instructions: Define fine-tuning: the model is further trained on thousands of your input-output pairs, changing its behavior.
List the three justified cases: distinct style, narrow domain with thousands of examples, cost cuts via a small model.
Note: in all other cases — prompting + RAG + tools.
Form the rule: if you don't have thousands of quality examples, fine-tuning is premature.
s2.validate: You can name the three scenarios where fine-tuning is justified and why.
s2.tip: No labeled data in the thousands means it's too early for fine-tuning.

s3.title: Why 90% of tasks are solved by prompting and context
s3.why: Most teams underestimate how far a good prompt with examples and pulled-in context gets you.
instructions: Take the task "AI replies in the CEO's voice" and solve it with examples in the prompt — few-shot.
Study [[node:prompting|prompt engineering]]: a clear role, style, and 3-5 examples of the desired answer.
Where knowledge is missing, pull it in via [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] rather than baking it into the model.
Compare timelines: prompt + RAG = result in a week versus a quarter for fine-tuning.
s3.validate: You understand why prompt + RAG is usually faster and cheaper than fine-tuning.
s3.tip: Run 50 prompt iterations first — then think about fine-tuning.

s4.title: Cost and complexity of fine-tuning
s4.why: The cost of fine-tuning isn't just training money — it's ongoing tech debt.
instructions: Count the direct costs: gathering and labeling thousands of examples, the training itself, infrastructure.
Add the hidden price: a new base model ships, your fine-tune is outdated, retrain from scratch.
Note the quality risk: the model "specializes" and may answer worse outside the training data.
Compare with prompting: switching models takes seconds, retraining a fine-tune takes weeks and money.
s4.validate: You can name at least three cost items of fine-tuning beyond the training itself.
s4.tip: Budget for repeating fine-tuning every time a new model ships.

s5.title: The tool-choice ladder
s5.why: The right order of tools saves months: start with the cheap and fast one.
instructions: Rung 1 — plain prompt: a clear instruction, a role, an output format.
Rung 2 — few-shot: add 3-5 input-output examples right in the prompt ([[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot prompting]]).
Rung 3 — RAG: pull fresh knowledge from your own documents ([[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]).
Rung 4 — fine-tuning: only if the previous three are exhausted and you have thousands of examples.
Climb up only when the current rung has provably failed.
s5.validate: You can recite the four rungs in the correct order from memory.
s5.tip: Never jump to fine-tuning skipping RAG.

s6.title: Common mistakes and the check
s6.why: The main trap is fine-tuning where a prompt would do; a quick checklist removes it.
instructions: Mistake 1: fine-tuning "just in case" from day one — climb the ladder first.
Mistake 2: expecting fine-tuning to make AI smarter — it only fits it to your data.
Check yourself with three questions: tried prompt and few-shot? tried RAG? have thousands of examples?
If any answer is "no" — fine-tuning is premature, go back to the ladder.
Record the verdict for your task: which tool is sufficient right now.
s6.validate: You ran your real task through the checklist and chose a tool deliberately.
s6.tip: Even one "no" on the checklist means fine-tuning is still too early.

sys-workflows-basics.title: What an AI Workflow really is — in plain terms
sys-workflows-basics.subtitle: Turn "AI helps me" into a repeatable process with predictable quality
sys-workflows-basics.whatItIs: An AI workflow is a stable chain "input → AI processes → result is checked → passed on" that runs the same way every day. It's not a single chat prompt and not just a trigger firing: it's a process where AI plays a specific role and you get a stable result without re-explaining context each time.
sys-workflows-basics.approach: The course moves from understanding "what it is and when you need it" to being able to assemble a working workflow yourself. First we tell a workflow apart from chat and from blind automation, then break down its anatomy (input, AI steps, a check point, output), then build a simple process for one task, test it on a real example, draw the boundaries and risks, and close with a readiness checklist.
outcomes: You tell a workflow apart from a one-off chat and from trigger-based automation
You see the building blocks every workflow shares: input, AI steps, check, output
You can assemble a simple workflow for one recurring task
You know which steps must never be handed to AI without human judgement
You have a checklist that tells you whether a workflow is ready for daily use or not

applyIn.title: Triaging an inbound stream
applyIn.description: Emails, requests, tickets arrive every day. The workflow reads, classifies, and drafts a reply — you just review and send.

applyIn.title: Preparing for routine events
applyIn.description: Meetings, reports, daily digests. AI gathers context ahead of time and writes a brief summary so you show up prepared.

applyIn.title: Standardizing team work
applyIn.description: When 5 people do the same thing in 5 different ways. One workflow sets a single process — quality stops depending on who runs it and in what mood.

pitfalls: Trying to build a "universal workflow for everything" — you get a monster nobody understands. Better to have 5 simple ones, each doing one thing well.
Automating a step that needs human judgement (e.g. "should I send this to the client") — sooner or later AI sends something inappropriate.
Building a workflow for a task that happens once a month — the setup won't pay off. The threshold is roughly 3+ times a week.
Removing the human check point for speed — you lose quality control exactly where a mistake costs the most.
Not fixing input and output explicitly — then it's unclear what the workflow eats and produces, and it can't be repeated or fixed.

exercises.question: Name three tasks you repeat more than three times a week. Which one is the best candidate for your first workflow, and why?
exercises.hint: Look for signs: "I'm writing this same prompt again", "I'm copying data back and forth again", the result doesn't depend on subtle judgement.

exercises.question: Take the chosen task and lay it out as a chain: what comes in, what steps AI does, where a human checks, what goes out.
exercises.hint: The simplest form is a [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]] A → B → C. No more than 4-5 steps for the first time.

exercises.question: In your chain, find the step that must not be handed to AI without a human check. Why is that one risky?
exercises.hint: Ask: what happens if AI gets this wrong and nobody looks? If the cost of error is high — that's a check point.

s1.title: What a workflow is and when you need it
s1.why: Without a clear sense of how a workflow differs from chat and from blind automation, it's easy to spend effort where a one-off prompt would do — or, the other way around, to do by hand for years what should long ago have become a process.
instructions: Memorize the core: a workflow = "input → AI processes → result is checked → passed on", the same way every day.
Tell it apart from chat: in chat you re-explain context every time — fine for a one-off, not for 50 repeats a week.
Tell it apart from blind automation: a workflow isn't just "a trigger fired" — AI performs a meaningful processing step inside it.
Check the applicability threshold: the task repeats more than 3 times a week, you catch yourself thinking "this same prompt again" or "copying data back and forth again".
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why a specific task of yours deserves a workflow rather than staying in chat.
s1.tip: If a task happens once a month — don't build a workflow, the setup won't pay off. Workflows live where there's repetition.

s2.title: How a workflow is built inside
s2.why: To assemble a process yourself you need to see its parts: every workflow breaks down into the same blocks. Whoever sees the blocks can fix and extend it, not just run someone else's.
instructions: Identify the four blocks of any workflow: input (what comes in), AI steps (what gets processed), check point (where a human looks), output (what's passed on).
Start with the simplest shape — a [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]]: A → B → C, no branches or loops.
For each step answer: what does it receive as input and what does it pass to the next step.
Mark where a human is mandatory: that's your future quality control point (more in [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gates]]).
Connect it to the bigger picture: a workflow is a special case of [[node:ai-workflows|AI Workflows]] and a building block of [[node:systems|Systems of agents]].
s2.validate: You can draw your workflow as a chain of blocks and point to where the input, the AI, the check, and the output are.
s2.tip: If you can't describe a step as "input → output", the step is stated vaguely. Split or sharpen it before moving on.

s3.title: How to assemble a workflow step by step
s3.why: Understanding without building stays theory. Here you turn the chosen task into a concrete working process — the main practical skill of the course.
instructions: Pick one recurring task (from step 1) — don't try to cover everything at once.
Describe the input as concretely as possible: where the data comes from and in what form (email, a row in a table, a message).
Lay out 3-5 AI steps as a [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]]: each step does exactly one thing.
Insert a human check point where the cost of error is high, not at the very end "for show".
Fix the output: where and in what form the result lands (a draft in email, a summary in Slack, a record in the CRM).
s3.validate: You have on paper a complete chain of input + 3-5 steps + check + output, and each step is clear without spoken explanation.
s3.tip: Make your first workflow deliberately small. A lightweight process that actually runs beats a "perfect" one you never launch.

s4.title: Walking through a live example
s4.why: A finished example shows how abstract blocks turn into daily value and gives a template that makes assembling your own easier.
instructions: Walk through the "prepare for a customer meeting" workflow as a reference.
Input: in the morning AI checks your calendar and takes the day's meetings.
AI steps: for each meeting it finds the customer profile in the CRM, pulls the latest email thread, writes a brief summary ("yesterday discussed X, open items Y, pain points Z").
Output: by 8:00 your Slack has summaries for all the day's meetings — you walk in prepared, not "hold on, let me remember".
Match the example's blocks to your own chain from step 3: does the input → steps → output structure line up?
s4.validate: You can explain which block of the example maps to which block of your own workflow.
s4.tip: Notice that the check is minimal here because the summary is only for you. The higher the stakes of the output, the stricter the check point must be.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: A workflow breaks not from complexity but from being handed something it shouldn't be. Knowing the boundaries separates a working process from a time bomb.
instructions: Don't build a "universal workflow for everything" — you get a monster nobody understands. Better several simple ones, each for its own task.
Don't automate a step that needs human judgement: leave the "send to the client or not" decision to a person.
Remember it's about predictability, not speed: the goal of a workflow is stable quality (9 out of 10 times the result is good), not just "faster".
Keep the check point exactly where a mistake costs the most — it can't be removed to save minutes (see [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gates]]).
Check the payoff: if a task is rare or changes a lot every time — a workflow doesn't fit it.
s5.validate: For your workflow you can name at least one step you deliberately did NOT automate, and explain why.
s5.tip: If you really want to automate a "dangerous" step, leave a draft + mandatory human confirmation there. That's the compromise between speed and control.

s6.title: Readiness checklist and validation
s6.why: A workflow counts as ready not when it "seems to work" but when it passes clear criteria. The checklist protects you from putting a half-finished process into daily use.
instructions: Check: input and output are described concretely — it's clear what the process eats and produces.
Check: each step does one thing and is phrased as "input → output".
Check: there's a human check point where the cost of error is high.
Check: the workflow covers one task, not everything at once.
Run the process on 2-3 real inputs in a row and compare the results — is it stable from run to run?
s6.validate: All five checklist items are met, and across three real runs the workflow produced a predictably good result.
s6.tip: Write down which input the workflow broke on or gave a weak result for — that's the first thing to improve in the next iteration.

sys-linear-chain.title: Linear Chain — a simple sequence of steps
sys-linear-chain.subtitle: A straight line A → B → C: the most reliable way to assemble an AI task
sys-linear-chain.whatItIs: A linear chain is a workflow with no branching: steps run one after another, each taking the previous step's output (A → B → C). No "if-then", no parallel branches. It's the basic form of a [[node:sys-workflows-basics|workflow]] and a special case of [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|prompt chaining]], where each step is a separate, understandable piece of logic. About 80% of real AI tasks look exactly like this.
sys-linear-chain.approach: The course moves from understanding "when a linear chain is the right call" to a working pipeline. First we cover the essence and the limits of applicability, then the mechanics (one step = one meaning, passing the result forward), then we build the chain step by step, walk through a live example, outline the risks and boundaries, and finally run a readiness checklist with a reliability check.
outcomes: You understand when a linear chain covers the task and when you need branching
You can split a task into clear steps following "one step — one meaning"
You build a chain where each step's output is correctly passed forward
You know where to put a checkpoint so an error doesn't travel down the chain
You can assess a chain's readiness with a checklist

applyIn.title: Content pipeline
applyIn.description: Receive an article → translate → check terminology → publish. Each step is debugged separately, and you see where it broke.

applyIn.title: Inbound processing
applyIn.description: Transcribe meeting audio → extract decisions → send to Notion. A straight line with no branching covers the whole task.

applyIn.title: Screening and scoring
applyIn.description: Read a resume → extract skills → match to a job → score. A sequence of steps = a transparent result.

pitfalls: Adding "if enterprise / if SMB" branching from the start — the workflow becomes unmaintainable. Better to have two separate linear chains.
Bundling several actions into one step ("read, summarize, translate") — debugging gets much harder. One step — one action.
Not passing the previous step's output explicitly — the next step works blind and produces garbage. See [[node:sys-context-passing|context passing]].
Sending the result to the user without a check — a step-3 error reaches the client. Put a [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gate]] before the final step.
Overcomplicating upfront "just in case" — start with a linear chain and add [[node:sys-branching-logic|branching]] only when you hit a wall.

exercises.question: Your task: incoming client email → identify the topic → draft a reply → send. Is this a good linear chain or do you need branching?
exercises.hint: Ask yourself: does each step follow the previous one without conditions? If "identify the topic" doesn't change the route ahead but just feeds the next step — a linear chain fits.

exercises.question: One step in your chain reads: "read the document, summarize, and translate to English." What's wrong with it and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: That's three actions in one step. Split it into three: read → summarize → translate. Debugging each separately becomes far easier.

exercises.question: Where in the chain "form → welcome email → checklist → contract draft → send" should you put a checkpoint?
exercises.hint: Before the irreversible action — sending. A Quality Gate right before the final step catches errors from all previous steps before they reach the client.

s1.title: What it is and when to use it
s1.why: Before building, you need to see that a linear chain is a deliberate choice of simplicity, not primitiveness. Most tasks don't need branching, and overcomplicating upfront wrecks maintainability.
instructions: Write the task in one sentence: what comes in, what comes out.
Check the linearity test: steps run strictly one after another, and the route doesn't change based on the data.
If "but what if…, then differently" comes up — that's a signal for [[node:sys-branching-logic|branching]], not a linear chain.
Set a rule for yourself: start with a straight line, add complexity only when truly necessary.
s1.validate: You can describe the task as "A → B → C" with no "if-then" in the route.
s1.tip: If you're torn between a linear chain and branching — starting linear is almost always right. Adding complexity later is cheaper than untangling premature complexity.

s2.title: How the chain works
s2.why: A chain's reliability rests on two rules: one step = one meaning, and a step's output is explicitly passed forward. Break either one and debugging becomes guesswork.
instructions: The "one step — one meaning" principle: each step does exactly one action.
The passing principle: step A's output is step B's input. Make it explicit, see [[node:sys-context-passing|context passing]].
Name each step with an action verb: "translate", "extract decisions", "score".
Make sure there are no hidden assumptions between adjacent steps — the next step gets everything it needs from the previous one.
s2.validate: Each step is described with one verb, and it's clear exactly what one step passes to the next.
s2.tip: If a step can't be named with a single verb — several actions are hiding inside it. Split it.

s3.title: Step-by-step application
s3.why: Now we assemble the chain in practice. Building from input to output guarantees each step gets exactly what the previous one produced.
instructions: List all steps in a column from input to output — that's the skeleton of the chain.
For each step, record what it takes as input and what it produces as output.
Check the joints: step N's output matches step N+1's input.
Identify the last, irreversible step (send, publish) — a check will go before it later.
Run the chain one step at a time, not all at once — that's how you see exactly where it breaks.
s3.validate: You have a list of steps where input and output are explicit for each, and the joints line up.
s3.tip: Run and test the chain step by step. If step 3 produces garbage, don't touch steps 4–5 until you fix step 3.

s4.title: A full chain example
s4.why: A live example shows how abstract rules turn into a working pipeline and exactly where a check goes in.
instructions: Walk through the "customer onboarding" example: form → welcome email → onboarding checklist → contract draft → send.
Trace how each step's output feeds the next: form data → email personalization → industry for the checklist → pricing in the contract.
Find the irreversible step — sending — and see why the check is needed right before it.
Imagine a failure at step 3 ("wrong industry in the checklist") and confirm only that step gets fixed, not the whole chain.
s4.validate: You can explain the example in your own words and show what is passed where at each step.
s4.tip: A good sign of a linear chain: when one step fails, you don't have to redo the rest.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: A linear chain isn't universal. You need to know when it stops working and which mistakes most often break even a simple chain.
instructions: Limit of applicability: if the route genuinely depends on the data — it's time for [[node:sys-branching-logic|branching]], not stretching the line.
Overloaded-step risk: several actions in one step → split them into separate ones.
Silent-failure risk: a step can return a bad result with no explicit error — you need [[node:sys-error-handling|error handling]] and checks.
Error-propagation risk: with no checkpoint, a step-N failure reaches the user.
Anti-pattern: premature complexity "just in case" — two simple chains beat one tangled one.
s5.validate: You can name at least 3 situations where a linear chain doesn't fit or breaks, and what to do in each.
s5.tip: When you want to add branching — ask: "does this cover 80% of cases or a rare edge?". A rare edge is often better split into a separate chain.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: The final pass separates "seems to work" from "works reliably". The checklist catches the typical gaps before launch.
instructions: Each step = one action verb (no bundled actions).
Joints line up: each step's output = the next step's input, context is passed explicitly.
The route is linear: no "if-then" in the transition logic.
A [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gate]] or manual check sits before the irreversible step.
The chain can be run one step at a time and you can immediately see where it broke.
s6.validate: All five checklist items are met, and on a test run you can pinpoint exactly what happens at each step.
s6.tip: If even one checklist item is open — the chain isn't ready for production. Simplicity yields reliability only with discipline.

sys-quality-gates.title: Quality Gates: checking before passing it on
sys-quality-gates.subtitle: How to catch AI errors early, while they're still cheap
sys-quality-gates.whatItIs: A quality gate is a point between workflow steps where the result is checked before going further. Either AI checks it against hard rules, or a human does. Without a gate, an error from step 1 slips into step 2, which feeds garbage to step 3, and the client confidently receives nonsense. A gate catches the error early: fixing at step 2 = a minute, explaining to a client later = a week of damage. This is the [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gates]] node in the [[node:systems|Systems]] section.
sys-quality-gates.approach: We move from understanding "why a gate and when" to a working checklist. First we see the mechanics of a check between steps, then we learn to define criteria (what exactly we check), walk through a real contract example, grasp the limits and risks (false passes, "AI checks AI"), and finally assemble a gate for our own task and verify it. Each step is short and checkable.
outcomes: You understand what a quality gate is and where it's actually needed versus where it just gets in the way
You can separate an AI check (by rules) from a human check
You can state concrete pass criteria for a gate on your own task
You see the main risks: false passes and the "AI checks AI" trap
You assemble a working gate before an action with consequences and verify it

applyIn.title: Sending documents to a client
applyIn.description: Before sending a contract or quote, the gate checks that all required fields are filled and amounts match the CRM. 95% goes without human involvement; disputed cases go to manual review.

applyIn.title: Writing to a database or CRM
applyIn.description: Before saving data, the gate checks format, required fields, and absence of duplicates. Garbage never enters a system that's hard to clean later.

applyIn.title: Financial operations
applyIn.description: Before charging money, the gate reconciles amount, recipient, and limits. An action with irreversible consequences never runs on an unverified result.

pitfalls: A gate at every step — the workflow becomes "AI 10 seconds → human 5 minutes → AI 10 seconds", nobody can stand it
"AI checks AI": if the main model made a mistake, the checking model makes the same one — you need a different principle (rules) or a human
Too strict a gate: it rejects correct results, the human is called constantly, and people start ignoring the gate
Too loose a gate: it lets errors through and creates a false sense of safety — worse than no gate
No clear return on failure: a result is rejected but with no note on what to fix — step 1 repeats the same error

exercises.question: In the workflow "generate a post → check → publish on social media", where do you put a gate and of what type?
exercises.hint: Publishing is irreversible. Which step has consequences? What can rules check (length, banned words), and what needs a human (tone, appropriateness)?

exercises.question: A manager set up an AI gate that re-runs the same model: "check if there are any errors". Why is this weak protection and what replaces it?
exercises.hint: Think about whether the model catches an error it made itself. Compare with a check by hard rules or a second human.

exercises.question: A gate before a database write rejects 40% of correct records. What kind of problem is this and how do you diagnose it?
exercises.hint: False pass or false reject? Look at the rejected records: are they truly bad, or is the criterion too strict?

s1.title: What a quality gate is and when you need it
s1.why: Without understanding "why", people put a gate either everywhere (the workflow dies) or nowhere (errors fly to the client). A gate is needed where an error is costly and can't be redone.
instructions: Memorize the definition: a gate is a point between steps where the result is checked before being passed on
List the actions in your process that have consequences: sending to a client, writing to a database, charging money, publishing
Mark where "we can easily redo it" — no gate is needed there
Accept the fact: AI gets things wrong 5-15% of the time, that's normal; the gate's job is to not let the error pass further
s1.validate: You have a list of 1-3 points where an error is genuinely costly and can't be redone
s1.tip: If unsure whether you need a gate, ask: "what happens if an error passes here?". If the answer is "nothing serious" — don't put a gate.

s2.title: How the check before passing on works
s2.why: A gate isn't just a checkmark "ok". It's a fork: passed → onward, failed → return with a note on what to fix. Without a clear return, step 1 repeats the same error.
instructions: Picture the gate as a fork with two exits: PASS (onward) and FAIL (back)
Decide who checks: AI by rules (fast, cheap) or a human (slow, but catches meaning)
For FAIL, describe what to return to the previous step: not just "error", but "field X is empty, fix it"
Tie failure to a human when AI can't cope — this is [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation to a human]]
s2.validate: You can draw the gate as a fork: condition → PASS/FAIL → where each outcome goes
s2.tip: The best return on FAIL is a machine-readable note: which rule was broken and what exactly to fix. Then step 1 doesn't repeat the error blindly.

s3.title: How to define pass criteria
s3.why: A gate without clear criteria is useless. "Check if everything's ok" is not a criterion. You need concrete, checkable conditions, otherwise the check is subjective and unstable.
instructions: Split criteria into rule-checkable (fields filled, amounts match, no duplicates) and those needing a human (tone, appropriateness, meaning)
State each criterion as yes/no: "all required fields are filled — yes/no"
For numeric checks set a threshold — this overlaps with [[node:sys-confidence-thresholds|confidence thresholds]]
Decide which criteria are blocking (FAIL = stop) and which are warnings (a flag, but not a stop)
s3.validate: You have a list of criteria, each stated as a checkable yes/no with a clear source of truth
s3.tip: First automate the rule-criteria (they can be checked by code) and leave the human only what rules can't catch. That keeps the workflow fast.

s4.title: Example: a gate before sending a contract
s4.why: A concrete example shows how two gates (AI + human) give 95% automation without losing control over the numbers. It's a template for your own task.
instructions: Step 1: AI generates the contract from the template and customer data
Gate 1 (AI, by rules): all required fields filled, amounts match the CRM, no duplicate paragraphs; FAIL → return to step 1 with a note
Gate 2 (human): the lawyer scans for 30 seconds → ok / not ok
If both gates pass → send; record the result: 95% of contracts without a lawyer, zero number errors
s4.validate: You understand why there are two gates of different types here and what each catches: AI — formal errors, human — meaning
s4.tip: A strong move is a two-tier gate: a cheap AI check filters out 95% of formal errors, and the human only steps in on the remaining edge cases.

s5.title: Limits and risks: false passes
s5.why: A gate creates a false sense of safety. If it's too loose, it lets errors through; if it's "AI checks AI", it catches the wrong things. You need to know where the gate doesn't save you.
instructions: Distinguish two failures: a false pass (something bad passed as ok) and a false reject (something good got rejected)
Avoid the "AI checks AI" trap: the checking model repeats the same mistake as the main one
For critical checks use a different principle: hard rules instead of AI, or a second human
Regularly reconcile the gate with reality — this is adjacent to [[node:sys-approval-flows|approval flows]] and overall workflow monitoring
s5.validate: You can name which errors your gate definitely does NOT catch, and where to back it up with rules or a human
s5.tip: Periodically take results that passed the gate and manually check a sample. If it contains errors, the gate is too loose and it's time to tighten it.

s6.title: Checklist and verifying your gate
s6.why: The final assembly: walk through the checklist and make sure the gate really works, rather than just sitting there for show.
instructions: Checklist: is the gate placed only before an action with consequences? (not at every step)
Are criteria concrete and checkable as yes/no? Is the source of truth specified?
On FAIL, is there a clear return with a note on what to fix?
Do critical checks go NOT through "AI checks AI", but through rules or a human?
Run 5-10 real results through the gate and verify by hand: is PASS actually ok, is FAIL actually bad?
s6.validate: All checklist items are answered "yes", and on the test sample the gate produced neither a false pass nor a mass false reject
s6.tip: A gate is a living mechanism. Return to the criteria when the task changes or new error types appear. Set up once doesn't mean forever.

sys-branching-logic.title: Branching logic in workflows
sys-branching-logic.subtitle: Make the model pick the route itself — via a decision schema, not if-else
sys-branching-logic.whatItIs: Conditional branching in an AI workflow: after step A, the model (not the user, not hardcoded if/else) decides which branch to take — B or C. Each branch is its own prompt, optimized for its task. The router picks the route: a separate classification call (often on Haiku), a structured output / tool use in the main call, or embedding similarity with no LLM. The key is an explicit decision schema: a closed list of options (enum), not free text.
sys-branching-logic.approach: The course moves from understanding why branching matters to a working implementation. First we see when a monolithic prompt should be split into branches. Then we design the decision schema and pick a routing method. We apply it in code, walk through a real helpdesk example, map the limits and risks (combinatorial branch explosion, missing default, ignored confidence), and finish with a pre-production checklist.
outcomes: Understand when a workflow needs branching versus a [[node:sys-linear-chain|linear chain]]
Design a decision schema: closed enum + confidence + reason + default branch
Pick a routing method (prompt-driven / structured output / embedding) for your latency and cost
Avoid the common failures: open text instead of enum, no default, ignored confidence, 15 branches
Build minimal router monitoring: branch distribution, accuracy, confidence distribution

applyIn.title: Customer support and triage
applyIn.description: One incoming ticket → refund / how-to / bug / feature-request → different prompts, different tools, different models. Router on Haiku, specialists on Sonnet.

applyIn.title: Email and input triage
applyIn.description: spam / sales / urgent → different actions. The structure and priority of the response depend on an input type you don't know upfront.

applyIn.title: Multi-stage AI pipelines
applyIn.description: Inside a large [[node:ai-workflows|workflow]], branching routes the input to the right specialist (security / style / logic in code review) instead of one do-everything prompt.

pitfalls: Open text output instead of an enum: the model writes "Refund Request" instead of "refund" and routing breaks. Always a closed enum via JSON schema or tool use.
No default branch: the router returns something unexpected, the code crashes. Always default to fallback or human escalation.
Ignoring confidence: a router at confidence=0.3 confidently routes the wrong way. Minimum: confidence < 0.7 triggers escalation.
Too many branches: 15 categories drop router accuracy below 70%. Cap at 5-7; otherwise a hierarchy router → sub-router.
Branching without logging the decision: a ticket lands in the wrong place and you can't inspect what the router decided. Log (input_hash, category, confidence, reason).

exercises.question: You have one prompt that "does 5 different things badly" across input types. Which two signals confirm it's time to branch, and where do you start?
exercises.hint: Signals: output structure varies by input type; you want different models per scenario. Start by writing the closed enum of possible categories.

exercises.question: The router returned category="refund" with confidence=0.35. What should the workflow do, and why exactly?
exercises.hint: confidence < 0.7 → don't trust the decision; escalate to a human or fall back, and log the reason. Otherwise the specialist runs a refund flow on the wrong case.

exercises.question: The business wants 18 ticket categories in one router. What's the risk and the architectural fix?
exercises.hint: Combinatorial explosion: the router gets confused, accuracy drops below 70%. Fix: a hierarchy — a top router into 5-7 groups → a sub-router inside each group.

s1.title: What branching in a workflow is, and when you need it
s1.why: Without branching, a workflow becomes either one giant do-everything prompt (unpredictable quality, expensive tokens) or rigid regex if/else that breaks on a new case. Branching gives each branch its own optimized prompt and localizes debugging.
instructions: Lock in the definition: branching is when the MODEL (the router), not the user and not hardcoded logic, picks the route after step A.
Compare with a [[node:sys-linear-chain|linear chain]]: if every input takes the same path, you don't need branching.
Check the applicability threshold: branching is justified at 3+ fundamentally different scenarios on the same input.
Write down 3 signals: one prompt "does 5 things badly"; output structure varies by input type; you want different models per scenario (cost).
s1.validate: You can name your real case and say how many fundamentally different scenarios it has on the same input (3+ or not).
s1.tip: If there are only 2 scenarios and they're nearly identical in structure, don't add a router — use one prompt with a parameter.

s2.title: Deciding the route: the decision schema
s2.why: The quality of branching is set by the decision schema, not the code. Free text from the router breaks routing about 5% of the time; a closed enum + confidence + reason + default make routing predictable and debuggable.
instructions: Write a closed enum of branches — 3-7, not 20 (e.g. refund | how-to | bug | feature-request | other).
Add a confidence: 0..1 field — the router's own certainty, for thresholds.
Add a reason: string field — a short justification for logs and debugging.
Build in a default branch (unknown / other) that leads to escalation or a fallback prompt.
Pick the routing method: prompt-driven (a separate Haiku call, cheap), structured output / tool use (one call, costlier, lower latency), or embedding similarity (no LLM).
s2.validate: You have, on paper, a router-response JSON schema with 4 parts: category (enum), confidence, reason, and a default branch.
s2.tip: Latency-critical? Use a structured output in the main call — one LLM hop instead of two. Budget-critical? A separate router on Haiku.

s3.title: Applying it: router + branches in code
s3.why: A schema with no implementation is useless. Here we assemble the working two-stage shape: a cheap router classifies the input, then code picks a specialized prompt and the right model/tools by category.
instructions: Step 1 — router: a Haiku call that returns strict JSON matching your decision schema.
Step 2 — confidence gate: if confidence < 0.7 → escalate_to_human(reason=...) before any branch is chosen.
Step 3 — dispatcher: a dict {category: specialist_prompt}, each branch with its own prompt + tools (billing_api, search_kb, etc.).
Step 4 — specialist: a Sonnet call with the chosen prompt; pass metadata {prompt_version, branch} for tracing.
Step 5 — cost optimization: router on a cheap model, specialists on a strong one — typically 5-10x cheaper than one big do-everything call.
s3.validate: Your code has two calls (router → specialist), the confidence gate sits BEFORE branch selection, and each branch has its own prompt.
s3.tip: Make the dispatcher a dict, not an if-elif cascade: adding a branch is one line, and the full route list is visible at a glance.

s4.title: Example: a SaaS helpdesk at 12k tickets/day
s4.why: An end-to-end example shows how the pieces fit at real volume: a Haiku router, five Sonnet branches with different tools, a confidence gate, and metadata for monitoring.
instructions: Read the router_prompt: "Categorize this support ticket. Return JSON: {category: refund|how-to|bug|feature-request|other, confidence: 0..1, reason}".
Trace the gate: routing.confidence < 0.7 → return escalate_to_human(ticket, reason=routing.reason).
Map branches to tools: refund→billing_api, how-to→search_kb, bug→linear_create, feature-request→feedback_log, other→general.
Note the metadata {prompt_version: 'router-1.2.0', branch: category} — without it you can't compute accuracy per version.
Read the data-driven rule: if 30% lands in other, that's a signal to add a new branch.
s4.validate: Using the example, you can explain what happens to a "give me my money back" ticket at confidence=0.9 versus confidence=0.4.
s4.tip: Stamp the branch and prompt_version immediately — you can't reconstruct after the fact which router version made the call.

s5.title: Limits and risks: combinatorial branch explosion
s5.why: Branching scales badly without discipline. The main risk is a growing number of branches and their combinations: router accuracy drops and the number of paths to test grows nonlinearly.
instructions: Keep the limit at 5-7 branches per router: at 15+ categories accuracy drops below 70%.
If you genuinely have more categories, build a hierarchy: a top router into 5-7 groups → a sub-router inside each group (not one flat 20-way enum).
Count the combinatorics: nested branching (branch → another branch) multiplies the number of paths; each path must be tested and logged.
Don't confuse branching with [[node:sys-loop-patterns|loops]]: repeating one step until a condition is a loop, not a new branch.
Always keep a default → escalation: an uncovered input must not crash the code or silently go the wrong way.
s5.validate: For your case you've named the branch count (≤7) and decided whether you need a router → sub-router hierarchy.
s5.tip: Before adding a 6th branch, ask: is this truly a new scenario or a sub-type of an existing one? Sub-types are better handled inside a branch than as a new route.

s6.title: Checklist and verification before production
s6.why: Branching breaks quietly in production without observability and guardrails. The final checklist closes the 5 common failures and fixes the minimal router monitoring.
instructions: Schema: the router returns a closed enum (not free text), with confidence and reason fields.
Safety: there's a default branch; confidence below the threshold → escalation/fallback; the code doesn't crash on an unexpected response.
Size: 3-7 branches per level; more than that → a router → sub-router hierarchy.
Logging: every decision records (input_hash, category, confidence, reason) plus branch and prompt_version.
Monitoring: a dashboard shows branch distribution, router accuracy (via human-review sampling), and confidence distribution.
s6.validate: All 5 checklist items are ticked; you can show where in production you'd see that 30% of tickets land in other.
s6.tip: Set an alert on the default/other branch share: its growth is the earliest signal that reality has diverged from the router's schema.

sys-loop-patterns.title: Loop patterns: refine until quality
sys-loop-patterns.subtitle: Refinement loops with a stop criterion and budget guards
sys-loop-patterns.whatItIs:
A single-pass prompt hits a ceiling: the model will not rewrite its answer "considering the issue found" unless you ask explicitly. A loop repeats a step (or chain) until a quality criterion is met or the iteration budget runs out — self-correction without a human.

Three canonical patterns: critique-revise (generator → critic → rewrite with feedback → repeat), a ReAct-style tool-use loop (think → call tool → see result → continue), and a convergence loop (two variants compared, agree in substance → finish). Every loop must have a max-iterations guard (3-10) and stop detection, or cost runs away.
sys-loop-patterns.approach: A loop without two guards is a bomb under your budget. First formulate a measurable stop criterion (compile, test pass, schema-valid, judge-score ≥ 8/10, embedding cosine > 0.92), then set hard limits: max-iterations AND a cost-cap. The critic must not be the same model with the same prompt as the generator — otherwise it cannot see its own errors. Log every iteration so you can tell where the model "got lost."
outcomes: Distinguish the three loop patterns and pick the right one for the task
Formulate a measurable stop criterion, not "until perfect"
Set dual protection: max-iterations + cost-cap, fail fast
Separate generator and critic roles so the loop actually improves
Log each iteration and read the iteration histogram as a health metric

applyIn.title: AI code generation / code review
applyIn.description: The target is working code, not "an attempt". A critique-revise loop adds +15-25% pass rate over single-shot at the cost of 2.5-3x tokens.

applyIn.title: Long-form writing with criteria
applyIn.description: Research reports and structured docs: a judge scores against a rubric, the generator reworks weak sections up to the score threshold.

applyIn.title: Multi-step agents
applyIn.description: Browsing, research, multi-step calculations: a tool-use loop thinks → calls a tool → sees the result → finishes, under a step limit.

pitfalls: No max-iterations: "iterate until perfect" — one edge case burns $50 and ties up a worker for 10 minutes.
The critic is the same model and prompt as the generator: the model cannot see its own errors (motivated reasoning).
Iteration cap exists but no cost-cap: a long context times 5 iterations = $5 per request.
A loop without logging intermediate steps: the final output is saved, iterations are lost — you cannot tell where the model got lost.
Convergence via text equality ("two outputs identical, finish") works 5% of the time; use semantic similarity or an LLM judge.

exercises.question: Take a task where the model's output is often "almost right". Formulate a measurable stop criterion for it — one you can check in code or with a judge call.
exercises.hint: If the criterion cannot be expressed as a number or boolean (passed / score ≥ N), it is not ready for a loop.

exercises.question: Design a critique-revise loop for this task in pseudocode: where the critique.score check goes, where cost > limit goes, where you return. Mark which model generates and which critiques.
exercises.hint: The critic should be cheaper than the generator (e.g. Haiku critiques, Sonnet generates) and use a different role in the prompt.

exercises.question: For the finished loop, name three metrics to log and an alert threshold for each.
exercises.hint: Iteration histogram (norm: 90% finish in ≤2), max-iter-hit rate (alert > 5%), cost-overflow rate (alert > 1%).

s1.title: Understand "refine until quality" and when it is needed
s1.why: A loop adds cost and complexity. Use it only when input varies and quality cannot be fixed in one prompt — otherwise it is overkill.
instructions: Write down your task and ask: is the output often "almost right", fixable in one revision?
Check whether a measurable quality criterion exists (compile, test, schema-valid, judge-score).
Compare: is the cost of an error higher than the cost of 2-3x LLM calls?
If yes to all three, the task is a loop candidate. Pick a pattern: critique-revise, tool-use, or convergence.
s1.validate: You can name the task, a measurable quality signal, and the loop pattern that fits it.
s1.tip: Code generation is almost always a loop: "working code" is a criterion, not "an attempt". See [[node:sys-workflows-basics|workflow basics]].

s2.title: Set the stop criterion
s2.why: Without an explicit criterion the loop either stops too early (low quality) or never stops. The criterion is the heart of the loop and is defined BEFORE the code.
instructions: Choose the signal type: binary (compile/test pass, schema-valid) or scalar (judge-score, embedding similarity).
For a judge, set a threshold: score ≥ 8/10. For convergence — cosine > 0.92.
Make sure the critic is a separate model or a radically different prompt, not the same generator.
Describe what happens when the criterion is met: return the current output + metadata (iterations, cost).
s2.validate: The stop criterion is expressed as a checkable condition (boolean or number with a threshold), and you know who evaluates it.
s2.tip: Calibrate the threshold on real data via the [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|eval suite]], not by guesswork.

s3.title: Assemble the loop and attach guards
s3.why: The stop criterion guarantees quality but does not protect the budget. Without max-iterations and a cost-cap, the first buggy case drains money and blocks a worker.
instructions: Set max-iterations: 3 for interactive (UX), 5-10 for async (research, code-gen).
Add a cost guard — a hard cap per request (3-5x average), fail fast on overflow.
Add a time guard: < 30s for interactive, < 5min for async.
In the loop body: generate → critic-check → if threshold met return; if cost/iter exceeded — return with an overflow flag.
Log every iteration: input, output, score, accumulated cost.
s3.validate: The loop cannot run forever: there is a max-iterations, a cost-cap, and a time guard, and every exit is logged.
s3.tip: Limits are about [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]]: one number ($X per request) saves you from a $50 bill.

s4.title: Walk through a working example
s4.why: Abstract rules come alive on concrete code. The code-review bot example shows how the criterion, limits, and logs come together in one loop.
instructions: Read the schema: MAX_ITER=5, QUALITY_THRESHOLD=8, COST_LIMIT_USD=0.50.
The initial pass generates the review with an expensive model (Sonnet); critic-call scores with a cheap one (Haiku).
Inside the loop: if critique.score ≥ threshold — return; if cost > limit — log_overflow + return with overflow=True.
Otherwise generate_review is rewritten with prior_review and feedback=critique.issues.
After MAX_ITER without success — log_max_iter_hit and return.
s4.validate: You can explain which code branch handles quality, which handles budget, and which handles observability.
s4.tip: Different models for generate and critic is not an optimization but a precondition for the loop to actually improve.

s5.title: Account for boundaries and risks
s5.why: The main loop failures are not quality but runaway cost and the illusion of improvement. Anticipate them at design time, not in production via the bill.
instructions: Infinite loop: always a hard max-iterations, no "just one more" exceptions.
Token spend: critique-revise costs 2.5-3x single-shot — bake it into your unit economics.
Motivated reasoning: a generator does not critique itself honestly — use a different model / role.
False convergence: text equality catches 5% of cases, use semantic similarity or a judge.
Loss of observability: without iteration logs, debugging is impossible.
s5.validate: For each of the five risks you have a concrete protective measure in the loop design.
s5.tip: A loop is controlled overspend in exchange for quality; keep it in check via [[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]].

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Before going to production you must confirm all guards are in place and the loop is observable. One missing limit equals a billing incident.
instructions: Check: the stop criterion is measurable and verifiable by code/judge.
Check: max-iterations, cost-cap, and time guard are in place.
Check: critic ≠ generator (different model or role).
Check: every iteration is logged via [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]].
Run on 20-30 real cases and collect metrics via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]].
s6.validate: On real data: 90% of requests finish in ≤2 iterations, max-iter-hit < 5%, cost-overflow < 1%.
s6.tip: If max-iter-hit is high, the criterion is too strict or the critic too weak; calibrate on data, not guesses.

sys-prompt-chaining.title: Prompt chaining: build a chain you can actually debug
sys-prompt-chaining.subtitle: 6 steps: break a complex task into a chain of prompts and pass data between them reliably
sys-prompt-chaining.whatItIs:
Prompt chaining is the technique where the output of one model call becomes the input to the next: `A -> B -> C`. Instead of one monster prompt — "extract -> classify -> write report" — you build three separate steps, each of which you can debug, cost-optimize, and validate independently.

This is not about the idea of sequential workflows (that's [[node:sys-linear-chain|sys-linear-chain]]); it's about the **mechanics of passing data** across boundaries: a schema at every junction, explicit handling of the previous step's errors, and reproducible results. This course is a practical walkthrough of how to build such a chain without ending up with a silently breaking system.
sys-prompt-chaining.approach: Design every boundary between steps as a contract, not as "I'll just pass the text along." A step's output is validated against a JSON schema before it reaches the next step — fail fast instead of a cryptic crash 30 seconds later. Pick the model per step (Haiku for extraction, Sonnet for reasoning) rather than one model for everything. And from day one, forward a `trace_id` through every call — without it, debugging a chain is impossible.
outcomes: You know when decomposing into a chain pays off and when it just adds latency
You can design a step boundary as a schema contract with validation
You know error-propagation strategies: skip / retry / fallback / escalate at each step
You can compute the cascade effect of errors (95% x 4 steps = 81%) and place [[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]] at boundaries
You build a reproducible, cheap, traceable chain with a `trace_id` and per-step logging

applyIn.title: AI research assistant
applyIn.description: Extract sources -> structured analysis -> write a brief -> critique. Different models per step, cached intermediate results.

applyIn.title: Document processing
applyIn.description: Parse a contract -> identify clauses -> flag risks. Validation at each boundary catches a failure before it reaches the final output.

applyIn.title: Support and auto-replies
applyIn.description: Transcribe -> analyze sentiment -> generate a reply, with human review between analysis and sending.

pitfalls: Passing raw text between steps instead of a JSON structure — the next step parses it with regex and breaks ~10% of the time.
Not validating step N output before step N+1 — once in 100 calls the model returns `null` instead of an array, and the crash arrives late with a cryptic error.
Using one heavy model at every step — Sonnet on simple extraction is a multi-fold overpay; pick the model for each step's task.
Ignoring error accumulation: at 95% per-step accuracy a 4-step chain is 81% end-to-end — without quality gates at boundaries this is invisible degradation.
Not forwarding a `trace_id` — logs show scattered calls you can't reassemble into a single request for analysis.

exercises.question: Take any 2-3-action task of yours ("summarize and translate", "extract and classify") and draw it as `A -> B -> C`. For each boundary, write down exactly which fields pass from one step to the next.
exercises.hint: If a boundary ends up as "the whole response text," that's a sign the schema isn't designed yet. Reduce it to the minimal set of fields the next step needs.

exercises.question: For your chain, spell out what each step does if the previous one returned an error or a weak result: skip, retry, fallback, or escalate to a human?
exercises.hint: Lean on [[node:sys-context-passing|sys-context-passing]] — you handle not just the successful output but also the signal about its quality.

exercises.question: Compute the end-to-end accuracy of your chain if each step works at 90%. How many steps make it unreliable?
exercises.hint: Multiply the per-step accuracies. 0.9 to the fourth power is about 0.66 — two thirds. Quality gates at boundaries raise this ceiling.

s1.title: What prompt chaining is and why to split the task
s1.why: One monster prompt — "extract entities, classify, write a summary, suggest actions" — works 70% of the time and fails 30%, and you can't tell which part broke. Decomposition turns a black box into a debuggable chain.
instructions: State it: prompt chaining is `A -> B -> C`, where one call's output becomes the next call's input (see the parent [[node:systems|AI systems]] and [[node:ai-workflows|AI workflows]]).
Write your task as one big prompt and underline the logically distinct actions in it (extract / classify / write / verify).
Each underlined action is a candidate for a separate step in the chain.
Note what splitting buys you: debugging steps in isolation, a per-step model, cached intermediate results, human review between steps.
s1.validate: You have a list of 2-4 logically distinct steps, and for each you can say what it takes in and what it returns.
s1.tip: If a task is a single action (just classification or simple generation), you don't need a chain — it only adds latency. Only split what genuinely consists of distinct tasks.

s2.title: How to pass one step's output into the next
s2.why: The main source of silent breakage is the boundary between steps. If step A returns prose and step B parses it with regex, the chain breaks about 10% of the time with no explicit error. A contract at the boundary turns that into a predictable fail-fast.
instructions: For each boundary, describe the output schema: `{field1, field2, ...}` via JSON schema or Pydantic.
Validate step N output against the schema before passing it to step N+1 — an invalid result stops the chain immediately, not 30 seconds later.
Pass the minimal needed set of fields to the next step, not the whole raw response (more in [[node:sys-context-passing|sys-context-passing]]).
Build in idempotency: re-running with the same inputs must yield the same result, otherwise you can't build a debugging story.
s2.validate: Every boundary in the chain has an explicit schema and a validation point before passing to the next step.
s2.tip: A schema at the boundary is also contract documentation. When step B starts getting an unexpected field a month later, the validator fails — not the business logic three steps downstream.

s3.title: How to apply it: design a concrete chain
s3.why: Time to move from a sketch to a working pipeline: pick the model per step, place the branching conditions and caching points. This is where the chain's real cost and speed get decided.
instructions: Assign a model to each step by the type of work: extraction/classification -> Haiku, reasoning/writing -> Sonnet, final critique -> Haiku. This is typically 3-5x cheaper than "Sonnet at every step."
For steps with deterministic prompts, add caching of intermediate results (e.g. Redis, TTL 1-24h) — re-running the final step becomes free.
Mind latency: sequential steps sum up (4 x 800ms = 3.2s); where steps are independent, consider [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|parallel fan-out]] instead of a strict chain.
Forward a `trace_id` through all steps and log each call separately (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging patterns]]).
s3.validate: You have a pipeline where each step has a defined model, caching behavior, and place in the overall latency.
s3.tip: Start with the cheapest model on each step and bump it up only where quality actually drops. Most often only one or two steps need the "expensive" model, not the whole chain.

s4.title: Example: a four-step research assistant
s4.why: A concrete example shows how schema, model choice, fallback, and trace_id come together into one working pipeline. It makes visible exactly where each rule from the previous steps kicks in.
instructions: Step 1 - extract sources (Haiku + web_search): get sources and immediately validate against `SourcesSchema` `{urls, snippets}`.
Step 2 - analysis (Sonnet): if fewer than 3 sources -> fallback response "insufficient data"; otherwise structured analysis against `AnalysisSchema` `{financials, leadership, products, risks}`.
Step 3 - write brief (Sonnet): assemble an executive summary from the structured analysis.
Step 4 - critique (Haiku): score the brief against criteria; if score < threshold -> one re-pass max, then return the result together with `trace_id`, `step_costs`, and `prompt_versions`.
s4.validate: Using the example, you can point out which boundary has validation, where the fallback triggers, and which step runs on which model.
s4.tip: The per-step `step_costs` log immediately answers "where is the money leaking," and `prompt_versions` answers "which prompt version introduced the regression." It pays off on the first incident.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: error accumulation
s5.why: A chain isn't free: step errors multiply, latency sums up, and without an error-handling strategy one weak step poisons the whole result. Understanding the limits separates a reliable chain from a fragile one.
instructions: Compute the cascade: at 95% per-step accuracy a 4-step chain is ~81% end-to-end; the longer the chain, the lower the reliability ceiling.
Place [[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]] at boundaries where the cost of an error is high, so a bad output doesn't move on.
For each step, set an explicit error-propagation strategy for when the previous step errors or returns low quality: skip / retry / fallback / escalate to a human.
Don't stretch the chain needlessly: extra steps add latency and lower total accuracy — only split down to the level of logically distinct tasks.
s5.validate: You know your chain's end-to-end accuracy and, for each step, you've defined what it does when the previous one fails.
s5.tip: If a 6+ step chain gives unacceptable end-to-end accuracy, don't blindly pile on retries. Either merge close steps or put a quality gate with human review at the riskiest point.

s6.title: Checklist and validation of the chain
s6.why: The final check catches the classic prompt-chaining traps before production: raw text at boundaries, missing validation, one model for everything, no trace_id. The checklist turns the course's knowledge into a repeatable ritual before launch.
instructions: Boundaries: every junction has a JSON schema and validation of the output before passing it on — nowhere is raw text fed to regex.
Models and cost: each step is on a model appropriate by cost/quality; deterministic steps are cached.
Errors: each step has a strategy for the previous one's failure (skip/retry/fallback/escalate); risky boundaries have [[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]].
Observability: a `trace_id` is forwarded through all steps, each call is logged separately (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging patterns]]); the chain is idempotent.
Run the chain on a "bad" input (empty/partial/invalid) and confirm it fails explicitly and early, rather than producing plausible garbage.
s6.validate: The chain passes every checklist item, and on a broken input you see the exact point of failure, not a mysterious error at the end.
s6.tip: Make this checklist part of code review for chains. Sharpen the prompting skills on individual steps via [[node:prompting|prompting]] — a strong chain starts with strong individual prompts.

sys-escalation-paths.title: Escalation to a human: when AI calls for help
sys-escalation-paths.subtitle: How to design handoffs so AI handles the routine itself and passes the hard cases on with ready context
sys-escalation-paths.whatItIs: Escalation is the moment AI says "a human is needed here" and hands the task off. It's not an admission of defeat but part of the [[node:ai-human-collaboration|AI + Human]] system design: AI closes 70-80% of tasks itself and passes the hard ones to a human pre-warmed — with gathered context, attempted solutions, and a recommendation. This course teaches you to design escalation triggers, format the handoff, and keep the balance without calling a human for every little thing.
sys-escalation-paths.approach: We move from meaning to mechanics. First we cover why escalation is needed at all and how a bad one differs from a good one. Then we design triggers — by task type and keywords, not by AI "confidence". We learn to format a handoff with a summary, apply it to a real scenario, examine the boundaries (over- and under-escalation), and assemble a checklist with validation. The running example is e-commerce support.
outcomes: You understand the difference between a bad escalation ("you figure it out") and a good one (with context and a recommendation)
You can design explicit escalation triggers by task type and keywords rather than by confidence
You format the handoff with a ready summary so the agent spends minutes, not hours
You distinguish over-escalation (calling for every little thing) from under-escalation (torturing the customer) and keep the balance
You have a checklist to launch escalation in your own system

applyIn.title: Customer support
applyIn.description: AI answers typical questions and passes complaints, refunds, and mentions of lawsuits to an agent with the conversation history.

applyIn.title: Handling requests and deals
applyIn.description: AI runs standard requests but escalates deals above a money threshold to a manager with calculation and recommendation.

applyIn.title: Internal AI assistants
applyIn.description: An AI helper on the team handles the routine but hands non-standard or risky requests to a responsible person with gathered context.

pitfalls: Escalating by AI "confidence" (confidence < 80% → call a human): AI is almost always confident, so it either doesn't escalate or does so randomly
Passing a "bare" task without context: the agent re-discovers what AI already knew
Over-escalation: AI calls a human for every little thing, people get overloaded, the point of AI is lost
Under-escalation: AI endlessly repeats failing attempts and annoys the customer instead of calling a human
No retry threshold: AI doesn't count its failed attempts and gets stuck in a loop

exercises.question: Why is escalating by AI "confidence" (confidence < 80%) a bad trigger, and what should replace it?
