exercises.hint: Recall how often AI is "confident" even when wrong. Think about what in a task is explainable and noticeable in advance.

exercises.question: Describe what AI should pass to the agent when escalating a complaint so the decision takes 2 minutes, not 20.
exercises.hint: Who the customer is, what the task is, what AI already tried, the recommendation, and a link to the history.

exercises.question: How can one system suffer from over- and under-escalation at the same time across different task categories?
exercises.hint: Think about what happens when rules are set crudely: somewhere the threshold is too low, somewhere it's missing entirely.

s1.title: Why escalate to a human
s1.why: Without escalation AI breaks in two extremes: it either dumbly repeats failing attempts and annoys the customer, or gives up at the first hurdle — then why have it at all. Escalation is part of the [[node:ai-human-collaboration|AI + Human]] design, not an emergency button.
instructions: State the goal: AI does 70-80% of the work itself and hands the hard 20-30% to a human pre-warmed
Write down the difference: bad escalation — "AI couldn't do it, you figure it out"; good — "couldn't do this specific thing, I gathered context, tried these options, recommend looking here"
Note that good escalation raises trust for everyone: customers, agents, management
Set your benchmark: the human should open the task and immediately get what's going on
s1.validate: You can explain with one example how "AI gave up" differs from "AI handed off the task pre-warmed".
s1.tip: Escalation isn't an AI failure but a sign of a mature system. Systems without escalation are more dangerous than ones that call a human on time.

s2.title: Escalation triggers: what fires the handoff
s2.why: The main mistake is escalating by AI "confidence". AI is almost always confident, so such a trigger either doesn't fire or fires randomly. Explainable triggers — by task type and keywords — work predictably. This is adjacent to [[node:sys-confidence-thresholds|confidence thresholds]] but is not replaced by them.
instructions: Build a keyword trigger list: "complaint", "cancellation", "refund", "lawsuit"
Add a retry threshold: AI failed twice in a row → escalation
Add risk and amount thresholds: deal above a money threshold → human
Mark task categories as "always human" (legal, medical, disputed)
Always honor the customer's explicit "get me a human" — it's an unconditional trigger
s2.validate: You have a list of 3-5 explicit, explainable triggers, and none of them sound like "if AI is unsure".
s2.tip: A good trigger can be explained in words to management and the customer. "Confidence < 80%" can't be; "mentioned a refund" can.

s3.title: How to format the handoff to a human
s3.why: The second common mistake is passing a "bare" task to the human without context. The agent spends time figuring out what AI already knew. A ready summary turns "an hour to figure out" into "5 minutes to make a call". This intersects with [[node:sys-approval-flows|approval flows]] when the human also approves the action.
instructions: Build the customer card: who they are, what the task is, order/ticket number
Describe what AI already tried and why it didn't work
Add status and signals: "3rd delay in 2 months, customer is angry"
Give a concrete recommendation: "refund + promo code"
Attach a link to the full conversation history so the human can dig deeper
s3.validate: Your handoff template contains: who, what, what's been done, the recommendation, and a link to the history — all in one message.
s3.tip: Rule: the human shouldn't ask the customer a single question AI already knew the answer to.

s4.title: How to apply: an end-to-end scenario
s4.why: Triggers and handoffs come alive only on a real flow. Let's trace escalation from the first message to the agent's decision using e-commerce support.
instructions: Customer: "my order didn't arrive" → AI checks tracking → stuck at sorting center → replies "order is delayed, delivery on such-and-such date"
Customer: "this is the third time, I want a full refund" → AI detects "refund" + "third time" → escalation trigger fires
AI prepares for the agent: "customer Ivanov, order #1234, 3rd delay in 2 months, previously ordered $50k, status — angry. Recommendation: refund + promo code. History: link"
Agent opens → immediately sees the context → makes a decision in 2 minutes
Check both outcomes: the customer quickly got a live person, the agent didn't spend 20 minutes on "tell me again"
s4.validate: You can walk through your scenario step by step and, at the escalation point, show which trigger fired and what summary went to the human.
s4.tip: Run scenarios out loud with a colleague playing an angry customer — weak spots in triggers surface immediately.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: over- and under-escalation
s5.why: Escalation breaks both ways. Too much — people are overloaded, AI is useless. Too little — the customer suffers, trust drops. The balance is held by rules, not by AI intuition.
instructions: Over-escalation: AI calls a human for every little thing → tighten triggers, remove extra keywords, raise thresholds
Under-escalation: AI endlessly repeats attempts → add a hard retry threshold and mandatory keyword triggers
Track the metric: what percent of tasks actually needed a human vs. what got escalated
Remember the AI boundary: it shouldn't make irreversible decisions (large refund, data deletion) on its own — that's always a human
Review triggers regularly: keywords and thresholds go stale along with the product
s5.validate: You can name which signal points to over-escalation and which to under-escalation in your system.
s5.tip: If you're torn between over and under at the start — choose slightly more escalations. Overloaded people are fixed by tuning; a lost customer is not.

s6.title: Checklist and validation
s6.why: Before launching escalation into your [[node:systems|AI system]], you need to make sure triggers are explainable, the handoff is complete, and the balance is tuned. The checklist catches holes before the customer does.
instructions: Triggers are set by task type and keywords, not by AI "confidence"
There's a retry threshold (e.g., 2 failures in a row) and amount/risk thresholds
The customer's explicit "get me a human" always fires
The handoff template contains: who, what, what's been done, the recommendation, a link to the history
Protection against over- and under-escalation is set up, and there's a metric to control the balance
s6.validate: All five checklist items are checked, and you've run at least one scenario from the customer's message to the agent's decision.
s6.tip: Reread the checklist through the agent's eyes: opening an escalated task, they should say "all clear", not "what even happened here?".

sys-approval-flows.title: Approval flows: human-in-the-loop
sys-approval-flows.subtitle: Embedding human approval before irreversible, costly, and risky AI actions
sys-approval-flows.whatItIs: An approval flow is a blocking mechanism: the AI proposes an action, a human approves or rejects it, and only then does the AI execute. It is not consultation but a gate in front of write operations in production. This course teaches you to decide which actions need approval, how to embed the gating point in the backend, and how to avoid turning approval into a formal rubber-stamp.
sys-approval-flows.approach: We move from motivation to implementation: first why approval is needed and how it differs from [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation]], then classifying actions by tiers, then the technical gate with dry-run and kill switch, applying it to a real scenario, examining the boundaries and anti-patterns (bottleneck, rubber-stamping), and a final readiness checklist.
outcomes: You understand the difference between approval (AI succeeded, needs permission) and escalation (AI failed, hand to a human)
You can classify actions into 4 tiers and decide what needs a hard gate
You can embed a blocking approval point in the backend with a dry-run preview
You know why kill switch, expiration, and a complete audit trail are needed
You recognize anti-patterns: approval fatigue, rubber-stamping, single-approver on critical actions

applyIn.title: AI customer-ops bot
applyIn.description: The bot issues refunds and emails customers. Tier depends on refund amount and recipient count: small — auto, large — 2 approvers.

applyIn.title: Infrastructure automation
applyIn.description: An AI agent deploys, restarts services, changes configs. Any production mutation waits for explicit approval before executing.

applyIn.title: AI-driven outreach and content
applyIn.description: The agent prepares a mass email or public post. Dry-run shows the audience and text, the human approves before sending.

pitfalls: Approval as UI only, no blocking gate in code — the button exists, but the AI executes anyway
A single approver on critical actions — a compromised account = disaster; you need 4-eyes (2+ approvers)
No dry-run preview — the approver sees no amount/context and stamps blindly (rubber-stamping)
No kill switch — during an incident there is nothing to instantly stop all write actions
Approval on every action, including trivial ones — approval fatigue, people approve everything, the guard fails

exercises.question: Classify by tier: (a) labeling a ticket, (b) a $300 refund, (c) deleting a customer account. Justify it.
exercises.hint: Tier depends on reversibility and damage scale. A label is reversible and low-stakes; a mid-size refund needs gating; account deletion is irreversible and destructive.

exercises.question: The bot's approval rate dropped from 95% to 60% in a week. What does this tell you about the system and what should you check?
exercises.hint: A low approval rate = the AI is poorly calibrated and proposes many actions people reject. Look at the rejection-reason distribution and changes in the prompt/data.

exercises.question: An approval request for a bulk update sat for 5 days and was then approved. What risk did you miss and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: The context went stale — data changed since the proposal. You need expiration: 1-24h depending on criticality.

s1.title: Why human-in-the-loop approval
s1.why: An AI with write access breaks production in minutes: deletes wrong records, sends a buggy mass email, approves refunds for 1000 customers. One bug compounds into disaster. Approval catches the error before the action.
instructions: State the difference: approval = AI succeeded, needs permission; [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation]] = AI failed, hand to a human
Fix the principle: approval is a BLOCKING mechanism (a gate), not consultation and not visualization
List the cost of having no gate on your project: which single AI action could cause the maximum irreversible damage
Connect to [[node:ai-human-collaboration|human-AI collaboration]]: the human owns the decision, the AI owns the execution
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence how approval differs from escalation, and name the worst no-gate scenario on your project
s1.tip: If an action is reversible and cheap to roll back, a gate may not be needed — a soft notification suffices. Do not gate everything.

s2.title: What needs approval: irreversible, costly, risky
s2.why: Without classification you either gate everything (approval fatigue) or nothing (disaster). The tier model splits actions by real risk and sets the gate's strictness.
instructions: Split actions on 3 axes: irreversible (delete, payment, email N>10), high-cost (compute > $X), high-risk (production deploy, customer-facing)
Map to 4 tiers: Tier 0 — no approval (read-only, label, draft); Tier 1 — soft (runs + notify + revert); Tier 2 — hard gating; Tier 3 — multi-approval (2+ approvers, 4-eyes)
Define thresholds via parameters: refund < $50 → tier 0, < $500 → tier 2, else tier 3
Note where soft approval is enough: internal actions, low-cost reversible, read-only research
s2.validate: You have a table of actions with an assigned tier and numeric thresholds where appropriate
s2.tip: Compare with [[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]]: tiers are a gradation of strictness, not a binary allow/deny.

s3.title: How to embed the approval point
s3.why: The gate must live in the backend and physically block execution. A dashboard button with no code-level block is an illusion of control. Dry-run and kill switch are mandatory parts of the approval point.
instructions: Put the kill switch check on the first line: `if not GLOBAL_KILL_SWITCH.enabled(): reject` — one flag `AI_ACTIONS_ENABLED=false` mutes all write actions
For tier 0 — execute immediately + log; for tier 1+ — create an ApprovalRequest and block execution until a decision (`await request.await_decision`)
Attach a dry-run preview: what, to whom (142 customers), cost ($0), reversibility (NONE), buttons [Approve][Reject][Edit]
Set expiration (1-24h by criticality) and required_approvals (2 for tier 3)
Write a complete audit trail to [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]]: action, params, approver_id, decision, ai_proposal_id, timestamp, trace_id
s3.validate: The code blocks tier 2+ until an explicit approve, the kill switch is the first check, and the dry-run preview plus the ai_proposal_id ↔ approval_id link are in the logs
s3.tip: Send the notification to an interactive channel (Slack Block Kit / email with buttons) so the decision is made where the substance is visible.

s4.title: How to apply it to a real scenario
s4.why: Rules come alive only on a concrete flow. A customer-ops bot with refunds shows all tiers, dry-run, multi-approval, and metrics in one place.
instructions: Define APPROVAL_RULES for your domain: refund by amount, send_mass_email by count > 10, delete_account → tier 3
Walk the tier 2 path: AI proposes a $300 refund → a request with preview is created → notify Slack → await decision → execute or reject
Walk tier 3: delete_account requires 2 approvers, and verify that a single approve does not execute the action
Set up metrics: approval rate (norm > 90%, otherwise the AI is poorly calibrated), median approval latency, rejection-reason distribution
s4.validate: On your scenario each tier behaves correctly: tier 0 auto, tier 2 waits for 1 approve, tier 3 waits for 2, metrics are collected
s4.tip: An approval rate below 90% is a signal about the AI, not the people: it proposes too much that gets rejected. Fix the calibration, not the gate.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: bottleneck and rubber-stamping
s5.why: Approval easily turns into either a bottleneck (everything waits for a human) or a fiction (people stamp without looking). Both extremes kill speed and protection.
instructions: Bottleneck: approval latency of 1min–1h does not fit urgent paths — those go either tier 0 (auto) or [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation]], not a blocking gate
Approval fatigue: gating trivial actions → people rubber-stamp everything → the guard fails. Gate only actually risky actions
Rubber-stamping without preview: "Approve refund #1234" with no amount or context = a formality. Always show what/to whom/cost/reversibility
Single-approver risk: one compromised account → disaster on destructive actions. Use 4-eyes for those
Stale context: a request with no expiration gets approved on outdated data → wrong action
s5.validate: You can name which actions should NOT go through the gate (urgent, trivial) and which 3 measures protect against rubber-stamping (preview, tier-based, expiration)
s5.tip: If the approver cannot explain what exactly they are approving, the preview is not informative enough. That is a dry-run bug, not a human one.

s6.title: Readiness checklist and verification
s6.why: Before production you must confirm the gate truly blocks, not just draws a button. The checklist catches the classic holes before an incident.
instructions: The gate blocks in the backend (not only in the UI): test that without an approve a tier 2+ action does NOT execute
The kill switch works: flip `AI_ACTIONS_ENABLED=false` and verify all write actions stop within seconds
The dry-run preview is complete: what, to whom, cost, reversibility — for every gated action
4-eyes on destructive: tier 3 requires 2+ approvers, a single approve does not execute
The audit trail is complete and links ai_proposal_id ↔ approval_id; expiration is set (1-24h)
s6.validate: All 5 checklist items are checked, and you ran the negative test: an attempt to execute tier 2 without approval is rejected
s6.tip: The best verification is a drill: flip the kill switch on staging and measure how many seconds it takes for all actions to stop.

sys-feedback-collection.title: Collecting feedback on AI responses
sys-feedback-collection.subtitle: Turning user signals into an improvement loop without fine-tuning
sys-feedback-collection.whatItIs: A systematic way to capture signals about AI response quality — explicit (thumbs up/down, ratings, comments, a "report problem" button) and implicit (regenerate, edit-before-send, copy, time-spent-reading). Every signal is tied to the response context: `prompt_version`, `model_version`, `response_id`, `user_id`, segment. This is the foundation of an improvement loop that improves the product through prompts and an [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|eval suite]], not through expensive fine-tuning.
sys-feedback-collection.approach: We move from understanding "why" to a built-in widget, then to the process "signal -> eval case -> prompt fix -> A/B -> roll out". Start minimal (thumbs), then implicit signals, then segmented analytics and calibration. At each step we keep privacy in focus and remember that feedback without an action process is dead weight.
outcomes: You understand the difference between explicit / implicit / behavioral signals and when each is useful
You can embed feedback collection tied to response context (prompt_version, model, segment)
You build a working loop: negative feedback -> eval case -> prompt iteration -> A/B -> roll out
You see data in slices (by feature, query type, segment), not just the overall thumbs rate
You avoid traps: negative-only bias, implicit-signal noise, PII leakage, premature fine-tuning

applyIn.title: Production AI feature from day one
applyIn.description: You ship a chat assistant or AI generation — add thumbs up/down immediately to catch bad responses in days instead of guessing why users silently leave.

applyIn.title: Improving without fine-tuning
applyIn.description: You have accumulated negative feedback — turn the top patterns into eval cases, iterate the prompt, and test against the suite. 90% of improvements come from here, not from training.

applyIn.title: Protecting valuable segments
applyIn.description: Overall 90% thumbs up, but enterprise tier 60% — segmentation reveals you are losing your most valuable customers while the average looks fine.

pitfalls: Thumbs only, no comment or context: "47% thumbs down" is useless — you do not know why
Feedback sits in read-only storage with no action process — the team loses motivation to provide it
Ignoring implicit signals: a 30% regenerate rate is a disaster, but "no one is complaining"
No segmentation — averages mask problems in expensive tiers
PII in comments without anonymization leaks into logs and training; plus jumping to fine-tuning after the first negative

exercises.question: Your dashboard shows 88% thumbs up, but the team complains about quality. Which two signals would you check first and why?
exercises.hint: Think about implicit signals (regenerate rate) and slices — the overall number hides problems in segments and query types.

exercises.question: You collected 200 negative feedback items in a week. Describe the path from that pile to shipping a fix without fine-tuning.
exercises.hint: Aggregate by patterns -> top issues into eval cases -> prompt iteration -> test against the [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|eval suite]] -> A/B -> roll out if pass rate improved.

exercises.question: Why is calibrating only on negative feedback dangerous?
exercises.hint: You fix edge cases and break the main path. You need a 1-5% positive sample to avoid negative bias.

s1.title: Why collect feedback on AI responses
s1.why: Without feedback you improve AI blindly: change a prompt "because it seems better," deploy, hope. Feedback gives ground truth — which responses are truly bad or good — and ties it to [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring metrics]]. "We shipped it, no one is complaining" does not equal "it works": 70% of users silently stop using it.
instructions: State which decision about your AI feature you are currently making blindly (without quality data)
Accept as fact: user silence is not a success signal but usually silent churn
Fix the goal of feedback: not "collect ratings" but "catch bad responses in days and have grounds for a fix"
Connect feedback to your existing [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]] — these are different layers: metrics say "it broke," feedback says "quality got worse"
s1.validate: You can name a concrete prompt/feature decision you currently make without data and explain which signal would justify it.
s1.tip: Feedback is part of [[node:ai-human-collaboration|human-AI collaboration]]: the user trains the system by flagging bad responses.

s2.title: Signal types: explicit and implicit
s2.why: Explicit signals (thumbs, ratings, comments) are precise but sparse — 1-5% of users give them. Implicit signals (regenerate, edit-before-send, copy, time-spent-reading) are noisy but dense — every user generates them. Behavioral (did they finish the task, continue the conversation) is closest to real value. Understanding the difference defines what and how you collect.
instructions: List your feature's explicit signals: thumbs up/down, 1-5 rating, comment, "report problem"
List implicit signals: response_regenerated, edited_before_send, copied_to_clipboard, time_spent_reading
Add behavioral: did the user finish the task, continue the conversation, convert
For each signal mark: precise or noisy, sparse or dense — this affects how much you trust it
Decide the starting minimum: explicit (thumbs) from day one, implicit from week two when you have a baseline
s2.validate: For your feature, at least 2 explicit and 2 implicit signals are listed with a precision/density note for each.
s2.tip: Implicit signals often catch silent dissatisfaction earlier than explicit: regenerate rate climbs long before anyone clicks thumbs down.

s3.title: How to embed feedback collection
s3.why: A signal is useless without context. Every feedback event must be tied to `(response_id, prompt_version, model_version, user_id, user_segment, context)` — otherwise you cannot slice by feature, prompt version, or segment when aggregating. The widget should be always-on and minimally intrusive to keep the response rate in a healthy 3-10% band.
instructions: Place an always-on widget on every response: 👍/👎 + optional textarea "what went wrong?"
On submit, store the full payload: response_id, feedback_type, comment, user_id, user_segment, context (prompt_version, model), timestamp
Attach event tracking to implicit signals: response_regenerated, response_edited_before_send, response_copied
Store everything (data lake / warehouse) with 12-24 month retention for training signal
Keep the response rate in a 3-10% band: higher means an annoying UI, lower means too little data
s3.validate: A test feedback event is recorded with full context (prompt_version, model, segment), and at least one implicit signal is tracked.
s3.tip: Tying to prompt_version is critical for the next step and for [[node:sys-versioning|versioning]] — without it you cannot tell which prompt version produced a bad response.

s4.title: How to use it: an improvement loop without fine-tuning
s4.why: Collected feedback is only valuable inside an action loop. 90% of improvements come from the "prompt + eval suite" pairing, not from fine-tuning. Fine-tuning is justified only when prompt engineering is exhausted and you have >10k high-quality examples. Without a "signal -> fix -> verify" process, feedback becomes dead weight.
instructions: Weekly, aggregate negative feedback into top patterns (by prompt_version, response type, segment)
Turn top issues into eval cases and add them to the [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|eval suite]] (5-10 new per week, target 50+ examples)
Iterate the prompt against the identified problem and run it against the eval suite
Run an A/B in prod, roll out the fix only if pass rate >= baseline (e.g. +2%)
Close the loop: record what exactly was fixed — that is the outcome of the weekly review
s4.validate: The full path from a weekly negative-feedback slice to shipping a fix is described, with an eval-suite check and a roll-out criterion.
s4.tip: Do not jump to fine-tuning after the first negative: it is expensive, slow, and easy to break. First exhaust the prompt + eval loop.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: bias, noise, privacy
s5.why: Feedback can easily mislead. Calibrating only on negative bias fixes edge cases and breaks the main path. Implicit signals are noisy — you cannot react to them blindly. PII in comments (customer names) leaks into logs and training. These boundaries define which signals, and how much of them, to trust.
instructions: Calibrate on positive too: sample 1-5% of positive feedback for human review, otherwise you only catch negative bias
Do not react to a single implicit signal — it is noisy; look at trends and thresholds, not individual events
Anonymize / redact PII before storage; give users an opt-out (see [[node:pl-privacy|privacy]])
Do not treat the overall thumbs rate as truth — it masks problems in expensive segments
Remember the limit: explicit feedback comes from 1-5% of users — a biased sample, not the whole audience
s5.validate: You can name at least 3 risks (negative-only calibration, implicit noise, PII leak) and a concrete countermeasure for each.
s5.tip: Privacy is not a formality here: feedback with customer names that ends up in training or logs without redaction is a real leak.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Feedback collection only lives as a closed system: widget + context + storage + a weekly action process + calibration + privacy. The final check guarantees no link is missing and that feedback actually moves quality rather than sitting as dead weight.
instructions: Widget: thumbs + optional comment on every response, response rate in the 3-10% band
Context: every event tied to prompt_version, model, user_segment; implicit signals tracked
Process: weekly aggregation -> eval cases -> prompt iteration -> A/B -> roll out by criterion
Slices: the dashboard shows not just the overall rate but slices by feature / segment / prompt version
Calibration and privacy: sample positive for review, PII anonymized, opt-out available
s6.validate: All five checklist items are achievable and verified on a real feature; there is at least one "feedback -> fix -> roll out" example that went the full path.
s6.tip: If any link is missing, feedback is incomplete: you either collect blindly or collect and never use it. Tie the whole loop to your [[node:systems|production-systems]] architecture.

sys-confidence-thresholds.title: Confidence thresholds
sys-confidence-thresholds.subtitle: AI answers on its own only when confident — below the threshold it asks, hedges, or escalates
sys-confidence-thresholds.whatItIs: A mechanism that lets the AI act autonomously only when confident enough, and below a set threshold switch to a hedged answer, a fallback, or escalation to a human. Without explicit thresholds a correct answer and a hallucination look equally confident, and the user cannot tell them apart. This course shows how to obtain a confidence signal, judge its unreliability, set thresholds with concrete actions, and calibrate everything against real data.
sys-confidence-thresholds.approach: We move from motive to working mechanics. First we establish why thresholds matter at all (without them an AI is "confidently wrong" as often as "confidently right"). Then we learn to get a confidence signal from three sources and immediately face its weak calibration honestly. Next we set thresholds with explicit actions per range, apply a composite score on an example, outline the limits and the risk of false calibration, and close with a checklist and validation. This is an infrastructure skill inside [[node:systems|production systems]] and part of [[node:ai-human-collaboration|human-AI collaboration]].
outcomes: Explain why, without confidence thresholds, an AI lies and tells the truth with equal confidence
Obtain a confidence signal from self-report, heuristics/log-probs, and a verification call, and understand its unreliability
Set thresholds (e.g. 0.8 / 0.5) with an explicit action per range: respond / hedge / escalate
Compute a composite score from multiple signals and apply it in the answer code
Calibrate thresholds on eval data and recognize false calibration and overconfidence

applyIn.title: Customer-facing factual answers
applyIn.description: Support answers and factual claims: high confidence — respond, medium — hedge and log, low — escalate, so you never "confidently lie" to a customer.

applyIn.title: High-stakes decisions and recommendations
applyIn.description: Financial, medical, legal, and regulatory contexts, plus decisions to act: the confidence threshold ties into [[node:sys-approval-flows|approval flows]] and [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation paths]].

applyIn.title: RAG assistants over a knowledge base
applyIn.description: The assistant answers from context: if confidence is below threshold it says an honest "I don't know" instead of inventing, and low-confidence answers feed [[node:sys-feedback-collection|feedback collection]] for calibration.

pitfalls: Trusting self-reported confidence without calibration — models are systematically overconfident (claim 0.9, accurate 0.7)
One threshold for every question type — a factual and an opinion question need different calibration
Setting a threshold with no fallback action — "confidence < 0.5" is undefined, so code crashes or returns a confused response
Hiding uncertainty from the user for "better UX" — it damages trust once the error is caught
Verifying with the same model (Sonnet judges Sonnet) — motivated reasoning, high correlation, low value

exercises.question: You have a single threshold of 0.8: above it respond, below it escalate. Escalations turn out to be 40% and the team is drowning. What do you change first, and why this rather than "nudge the threshold by gut"?
exercises.hint: First check calibration: does claimed confidence match real accuracy. You likely need a middle hedge range, segmentation by question type, and an A/B measurement — not an arbitrary threshold shift.

exercises.question: In self-report the model consistently rates itself 0.9, but on a labeled sample it is accurate in 65% of cases. What is this called and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: This is overconfidence / false calibration. You need a calibration process: sample 200 responses across buckets, human-label correctness, plot confidence vs accuracy, and adjust thresholds; plus a composite with an independent verification signal.

exercises.question: Why is a composite score from self-report + verification + log-probs more reliable than any single signal?
exercises.hint: Each signal fails in its own way: self-report can lie, log-probs aren't always available, verification is expensive. The composite is robust to a single-signal failure — but verification must be a different model/framing.

s1.title: Why confidence thresholds matter
s1.why: Without explicit thresholds an AI "confidently produces nonsense" as often as it is confidently right: a correct answer and a hallucination look identical, and the user cannot tell them apart — a direct hit to trust.
instructions: State the problem: a correct answer and a hallucination are indistinguishable by tone → the user cannot judge the risk.
Describe what a threshold gives: the AI explicitly says "not sure," escalates, or falls back to a conservative answer.
Lock in the trade-off: worse UX in edge cases, but longer-lasting trust → more adoption.
Connect to context: this is infrastructure for [[node:systems|production systems]] and part of [[node:ai-human-collaboration|human-AI collaboration]].
s1.validate: You can explain in two sentences why "confidently wrong" is more dangerous than a visible error and what a threshold changes.
s1.tip: The goal is not to remove uncertainty but to make it visible and managed — an honest "I don't know" beats a polished but false answer.

s2.title: Getting a confidence signal and why it's unreliable
s2.why: To set a threshold you need a numeric confidence signal. But all three sources are imperfect, and ignoring their weakness is the classic beginner mistake.
instructions: Log-probs: token probabilities; low ones on key tokens → the model is uncertain. Not every API exposes them (Anthropic — partially via structured outputs).
Structured self-report: ask the model to return `{answer, confidence: 0..1, reasoning}`. Cheap, but calibration is weak.
Verification call: a separate LLM call scores confidence against criteria. More expensive but better calibrated.
Remember the key limit: models are systematically overconfident — claimed confidence ≠ real accuracy.
s2.validate: You can name the three signal sources, their cost, and why none can be trusted blindly without calibration.
s2.tip: Self-report can lie; log-probs are a structural signal. Where available, combine both rather than picking one.

s3.title: Setting the threshold and the low-confidence action
s3.why: A threshold with no explicit action is useless: "confidence < 0.5 — then what?" makes the code crash or return a confused response. Every range needs a defined outcome.
instructions: Set the ranges: > 0.8 → respond directly; 0.5–0.8 → hedge ("Based on what I know…") + log for review; ≤ 0.5 → escalate or an honest "I don't know."
Define an explicit fallback action for each range — no undefined branches.
Tie the low range to [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation paths]] and decisions to act via [[node:sys-approval-flows|approval flows]].
Account for segmentation: factual and opinion questions may need different thresholds.
s3.validate: For each of the three confidence ranges you have a concrete action defined, and the "low confidence" branch is not left empty.
s3.tip: Start with the 0.8/0.5 defaults, but treat them as a hypothesis for calibration, not as truth.

s4.title: Applying it: a composite score in the answer code
s4.why: A single signal is fragile. A composite score from several sources is robust to any one failing and yields thresholds you can trust in production.
instructions: Collect the primary answer with self-report `{answer, confidence, confidence_basis, uncertainty_factors, sources}`.
Make a verification call with a different model (e.g. Haiku judges Sonnet) — a separate verification_score.
Compute composite as a weighted average biased toward verification, e.g. `0.4*confidence + 0.6*verification_score`.
Route on composite: > 0.8 — answer; 0.5–0.8 — answer with uncertainty_factors; ≤ 0.5 — escalate_to_human.
Track metrics: composite distribution, escalation rate (target 5–15%), reduction in "confidently wrong."
s4.validate: Your code returns a different outcome for the three composite ranges and logs low-confidence answers for later calibration.
s4.tip: Verification must use a different model or radically different framing — otherwise the model just justifies itself.

s5.title: Limits and risks: false calibration
s5.why: The nastiest failure is not the absence of a threshold but a threshold trusted in vain: claimed confidence doesn't match real accuracy, and the whole logic quietly falls apart.
instructions: Recognize false calibration: the model claims 0.9 but is accurate at 0.65 — the thresholds become meaningless.
Run a calibration process quarterly: sample 200 responses across buckets → human-label correctness → plot confidence vs accuracy → adjust.
Calibration target: 80% claimed confidence ≈ 80% real accuracy (±5%).
Don't tune thresholds "by gut": any change → A/B test → measure → roll back if there's no gain.
Don't hide uncertainty for UX — an honest hedge wins in the long run.
s5.validate: You can describe how to check calibration on data and why shifting a threshold without measurement is more dangerous than it looks.
s5.tip: Sample low-confidence answers more often into [[node:sys-feedback-collection|feedback collection]] — they yield the most valuable calibration data.

s6.title: Checklist and validation
s6.why: The final assembly: thresholds work only as a system — signal, action, composite, calibration, and metrics together. The checklist catches gaps before production.
instructions: Signal: a confidence source(s) is chosen, with its cost and unreliability understood.
Thresholds and actions: each range has an explicit outcome, and the low-confidence branch leads to [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation]].
Composite: verification by a separate model/framing, and the composite score routes the answer.
Calibration: there is a quarterly confidence-vs-accuracy process and a rule to change a threshold only via measurement.
Metrics: escalation rate within the target band (5–15%), "confidently wrong" tracked, linked to [[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]].
s6.validate: All five checklist items are ticked, and on test requests different confidence levels produce different, predefined outcomes.
s6.tip: If any item is "on paper" without measurement, it's still a hypothesis, not a threshold. Calibrate first, trust second.
